newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Gunfire erupts near disputed Bosnia village.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire erupts near disputed Bosnia village.

text.p: Shooting and explosions erupted near the contested village of Gajevi in northeastern Bosnia on Tuesday, but U.N. and NATO sources could not confirm Moslem claims that returning refugees were under Serb attack.
"Gunfire and multiple explosions were heard from the vicinity of Gajevi this morning at about 0740 hours," Alexander Ivanko, Sarajevo spokesman for the U.N. police force, said.
"We do not have U.N. police monitors in the village so we are unable to say exactly what is happening."

A Bosnian Moslem refugee official faxed news agencies a statement saying that Moslems who had returned to Gajevi on Serb territory on Monday had come under fierce attack from Serb forces on Tuesday morning.
The fax said there had been Moslem casualties but did not specify how many.
A spokesman for NATO-led peace forces in Bosnia, Major Brett Boudreau, acknowledged reports of shots and explosions but could not confirm that Serbs were attacking.
"The situation is fluid and there is evidence to suggest that there is sporadic fire going on. We are taking action to restore calm in the area," Boudreau told Reuters in Sarajevo.
"We are not necessarily saying that it is Serbs attacking Moslems. That does not jibe with the information we have."
Boudreau said NATO had no forces in the village but that there was, at a minimum, a Russian company and some U.S. forces in the area as well as U.S. Apache helicopters circling above.
"We are deploying an additional number of U.S. troops into the area," Boudreau said.
A spokeswoman at NATO's Task Force Eagle base in Tuzla said a Quick Reaction Force had been deployed into the Gajevi area on Tuesday morning once gunfire was reported.

She explained that communications were so poor in the area that members of the quick reaction team might have to return to Tuzla before a reliable account of what's happening on the ground would be available.

As many as 600 Moslems crossed the Inter-Entity Boundary Line (IEBL) northeast of Tuzla on Monday in a bid to return to homes in Gajevi and Koraj, on Serb-administered territory, from which they were driven during the Bosnian war.
Some shots were fired on Monday and at least one Serb was reported to have been wounded. An unarmed U.N. police monitor was also wounded when a Serb policeman's handgun discharged accidentally.
Under the Dayton peace accord which ended the Bosnian war one year ago the IEBL is supposed to be an administrative boundary line between Moslem-Croat and Serb territory.
Instead it has hardened into a de facto border across which refugees have been unable to return to homes located in areas controlled by rival ethnic groups.
At least 60 Moslems, many of them women and children, had vowed to spend the night in Gajevi in tents they brought to the destroyed village.
NATO forces and U.N. police who moved into the area on Monday took up positions nearby overnight to keep the peace.
